-— Presented at Traiming Course June 6/51. 


( K&MP KANAWANA HISTORY - 1951 


It was in the year 1892 that Y.M.C.A. camping for boys in Montreal 
got its start. During that summer Mre De Ae Budge, the General Secretary of 
the Association, made a fishing trip te Lae Des Isles. Mre De We Ross, a 
Direetor of the Association, accompanied Mr. Budgee The train at that time 


went only to Ste Jerome - beyond that the trip was made by horse and carte 


It was just at this time that camping for boys was being discussed 
by Associstion Secretaries and Boardse A few Associations had opened campse 
Mr. Budge and Mr. Ross were greatly impressed by the Laurentian countrye They 


talked about the possibilities of a eamp for boys and young mene 


In the fall of 1892 a Committee of Messrse JeWe Ross, WeEe Cushing, 
WeWe Wilson, Te Duncan Patton and WeHe Ball, was appointede Plans were laid 
during the fall and winter months. Im the sprimg of 1893 a trip was mde to 
the Stee Agathe region, the area was explored. At that time little was known 
of the region and this group of "Gentlemen Adventurers" toured the country 
over “Cordurey" roads in buckboards and thoroughly investigated the lakes and 


islands by boate 


After much searching a site was chosen on Lac St. Joseph at Ste 
Adolphe de Howard - the islands seemed an excellent spot for a camp and at 
that time the shores were heavily wooded and had not been swept by fire - 


the fishing was excellent. 


And so plans were made for the first campe The equipment consisted 
of six tents - a marquee for a dining tent - all cooking was done over an 


open firee 


Ze 


During the summer of 1900 the attendance was thirty-seven boys 
and seventy-two young mene The dining marquee had been replayed by a log 


cabin and kitchen at a cost of $700ce00. 


During the following years interest grew rapidly in the camp, and 
it was recognized by Association leaders that one camp could not house both 
boys and young mene Early in 1910 a Committee under the Chairmanship of 


Mre ReLe Charlton was constituted te leok for a new site for the boys’ campe 


During the late winter months of 1910 Mr. Charlten and his Comm~ 
ittee of Messrs. ReBe Ross Jre, and Le Cushing mde a trip to the Laurentians 
to choose the camp site. After some searching the group arrived at St. Sauv= 
eur and commenced to walk at night over the hills to Lac Maroise Running 
inte a rain and snow storm the Committee lost its way and stayed overnight at 
a farmhouse. The next day the country was explored and Lake St. Louis, the 


present site, was locatede 


Great foresight was shown by the Committee in suggesting the pur= 


chase of all the shore line on the lakee 


A short time later Mre Je We McConnell purchased the land around 
Lake Desjardins. This he presented te the Y.M.C.A., and the lake was ren- 


owned “Lake Wilson" after Mr. McConnell's sone 


A great deal of thought was given to choosing a name for the ecempe 
Mr. Charlton suggested Kanawana which was like the name of a Furness Steamere 


At a later meeting the name Kanawana was adopted, which means in the Indian 


-je 


language “lots to eat". The first prospectus therefore called the Kamp 
Kanawanae The name of the lake was alse sb from Ste Louis to Lake 


Kanawanae 


The true story of the early days would not be complete without 
pointing out to use Mr. Charleton's own words, "That a great deal of prayer 
and waiting on God was engaged in while the camp was being chosen and 
equipped, and there is no doubt that God's hand was in it, judging by the 


success which has since attended the eampe" 


In the years following the opening of the camp, additional prop-=- 
erty was purchased so that today the cemp encompasses all of Lakes Kanawana, 
Wilson, and Round Lake, plus a sizeable part of the shoreline on Lake 


Becsiee 


With the purchase of the property expansion plans were mde which 
necessitated carving the camp out of the rugged wilderness of rock and 
foreste Bushland had to be cleared = rocks removed, ground levelled for 


tents « playing fields, a road built - buildings - wharves, etce 


Early during the camp the lewer pavilion on the lake front was 
constructed. In 1920 the present dining hall and kitchen unit was completede 
In 1927 the lodge and museum was builte In 1936 the Bantam cabins were 
erectede In 1938 the water system and latrines constructed, 1939 the showers 
installede In 1942 the’ Junior cabins were built and fourteen new tent plat- 
forms constructed for the Intermediate and Senior campse Canvass cots were 


introduced throughout the Senior, Intermediate, and Junior campse 


whe 


In the fall of 1942 the Camp board reviewed the housing accomm= 
odation and embarked upon a building cempaign to construct seven new opene 
sided cabins in the Junior Section of the camp, and fourteen new tent plat- 
forms in the Intermediate and Senior Seetions of the campe Much consider= 
ation was given to structural design and layout of the new units, and under 
the supervision of Mr. Ross Wiggs, plans were finalized early in October. 
Permission was secured from the construction controller to embark upon the 
building program and the lumber and other supplies ordereds Ee Ce Page 


undertook the contract of building the structurese 


Mr. Roy Locke became Camp Chief during the summer of '47. Since 
that time several new inovations have developed such as a completely new 
main wharf, new cabimefor the Senior Seetien Director, electrification of 
the camp with a new automatic water system with controlled chlorination, and 


electric refrigeratione 


Plans are now underway to build a new boat house to replace the 
lower pavillione It is planned to construct this boat house next Septembore 
those of yeu who will be back with us next year will have the advantage of 


using this new facility. 


The story above has concerned mainly buildings and equipment, but 
never let us forget that these are merely land marks on the road to building 
fine Christian Charactere The physical development of the property only 
suggests that year by year the camp is improvinge If ow program and leader- 


ship had not retained its fine calibre through the years, Kanawana could net 


-5e 


have continued as longe All of us in this room have an opportunity of 


writing another page in the history book of Manawana. Let us try to make 


this page the brightest in the booke
